 2026 Election Democrat Mary Peltola flips Alaska Senate seat, defeating GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan
 NBC News projects that Peltola eclipsed 50% of the vote needed to avoid a ranked choice tally, a victory that will give her party a 56-44 Senate majority next year. 
 Democrat Mary Peltola wins Alaska’s Senate race, NBC News projects 06:31 Get more news Live on Share Add NBC News to Google Nov. 17, 2026, 10:19 PM EST  /  Updated   Nov. 17, 2026, 11:07 PM EST By Jonathan Allen Democrat Mary Peltola defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, NBC News projects, pushing her party’s Senate majority to 56 seats after a stunning wave election.
 Her party ultimately flipped nine seats in this year’s midterm elections, all but one in states President Donald Trump carried in 2024. 
 Peltola, a former House member, had previously been elected statewide twice before losing her seat two years ago. Now, her Senate victory bolsters a Democratic caucus that will also include members from the likes of Kansas, Mississippi, South Carolina and Texas, forming the largest Senate majority either party has had in 16 years .
 In a statement Tuesday night, Peltola said she will fight for Alaskans in the Senate.
 “From Juneau to Utqiagvik, the message from Alaskans is clear: the status quo in DC is not working for Alaska,” Peltola said. “As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.”
 “As our next United States Senator, I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska’s working families,” she said.
 Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., celebrated Peltola’s projected victory and the wider margin it brings.
 “With 56 seats, Democrats are in a prime position to create a durable majority that can create lasting, real results for the American people,” he wrote on X . “We must earn back trust by passing bills that lower costs and improve lives — and dare Donald Trump to veto them at his own peril. We will be relentless. This is just the beginning.”
 Democrats’ 56-seat Senate total will include two independents who caucus with the party: Sens. Angus King of Maine and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.
 Peltola’s win comes after the Alaska race was roiled in the final days by investigations into allegations of ballot stacking, with a legal battle over a potential spoiler candidate intensifying ahead of Election Day.
 NBC News reported in July that state and federal prosecutors were investigating the candidacy of Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher and political newcomer who Republicans suspected had been recruited by Democrats to siphon votes from the incumbent, listed as Dan S. Sullivan on Alaska’s ranked choice ballot.
 Alaska utilizes a voting system in which the top four candidates from the all-party primary advance to the general election. Voters then rank the candidates in order of preference. If no candidate receives an initial majority, the fourth-place finisher will be eliminated, and that candidate’s supporters will have their second-choice votes counted. If none of the remaining candidates has more than 50% after that, the same process will repeat for the third-place finisher.
 Since Peltola won a majority on the first ballot, the race did not go to ranked choice tabulation, which means any confusion over the two Sullivans did not affect the result.
 A spokesperson for Sen. Sullivan’s campaign said in a statement Monday that Alaskans “deserve a complete and accurate count, and we will let that process run its course until every legal vote is counted and certified.”
 “We will not be commenting on individual ballot updates or outside projections in the meantime,” campaign spokesperson Nate Adams said. “The campaign will have more to say by the end of this week.”
 In October, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit aimed at blocking Alaska from certifying the results if the GOP senator lost, a move that Trump told reporters he had ordered.
 Several days later, The New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign was involved in recruiting the other Sullivan to run. Peltola has denied involvement in Dan J. Sullivan’s campaign, and he has also said it was his own decision to run.
 In the wake of the report, Trump called for Peltola to be prosecuted, and the Justice Department said it would redouble its efforts to investigate whether any federal laws were broken. The weekend before Election Day, a federal judge dismissed the Trump administration’s effort to segregate ballots cast for Dan J. Sullivan.
 GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy also ordered a state investigation into Peltola’s campaign.
 Alaska has not voted for a Democrat for president since 1964, before both Sullivan, 61, and Peltola, 53, were born, and its other Senate seat has been held by a member of the Republican Murkowski dynasty since 1981.
 But Peltola had won statewide before, having taken Alaska’s at-large House seat in a special election in 2022 and winning one full term that same year. She lapped Sullivan in direct fundraising — $37 million to $14 million through mid-October — which was a constant reminder throughout each quarterly reporting period that she was a formidable challenger.
 Peltola ran the same playbook as Democrats across the country, yoking Sen. Sullivan to Trump. Though Trump won Alaska three times by double-digit margins, he never reached 55% of the vote. And his second-term policies proved as unpopular in the Last Frontier State as they did with voters in the Lower 48, giving Peltola plenty of room to hammer Sullivan on overall inflation, the Iran war and fuel costs.
 “Dan’s part of a rigged system where politicians get wealthy and you get hurt,” she said in one ad. “They make cash while our diesel prices go up, our healthcare prices keep rising, and we have fewer fish in our rivers.”
 Sullivan portrayed Peltola as a tool of Washington Democrats and as a lawmaker in name only. If she made a campaign commercial listing her accomplishments, he said, “that would be the shortest ad in American history.” None of her bills became law, and only one, which would have created a food-security office in the Department of Veterans Affairs, passed in the House.
 Trump’s efforts to bolster Sullivan included a mid-October campaign visit. But the national wind blew straight across the country to Alaska, and Peltola emerged victorious.
